content: Assistive products, including prosthetic and orthotic devices, are essential for maintaining or improving individual functionality. These products should be made available at a cost that is affordable for the community or country. The list of such products is not restrictive but serves as a model for governments to create their own national lists. This model can encourage governments to fulfill their obligations under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) by ensuring access to assistive products at an affordable cost. Additionally, the list can raise public awareness, mobilize resources, guide product development, and stimulate competition, ultimately increasing global access to assistive products. Governments can use this model to define prosthetic, orthotic, and mobility products, as well as the 37 standards for prosthetics and orthotics outlined in the implementation manual. These decisions are critical for addressing the significant unmet and growing needs in this area, advancing universal health coverage, and establishing reimbursement policies, including insurance coverage. Of the 50 assistive products on the WHO priority list, 16 are mobility devices, encompassing six categories central to prosthetics and orthotics services. The 16 mobility products on WHO’s priority list include lower-limb orthoses, upper-limb orthoses, spinal orthoses, clubfoot braces, lower-limb prostheses, therapeutic footwear (for diabetic, neuropathic, and orthopedic conditions), canes, sticks, crutches, standing frames, walking frames, walkers, rollators, tricycles, and various types of wheelchairs (manual for active use, manual assistant-controlled, manual with postural support, and electrically powered). The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) is an independent international NGO that develops standards to facilitate global trade and ensure quality, safety, and efficiency. ISO standards cover a wide range of industries, including healthcare and assistive products. For prosthetics and orthotics, ISO standards such as ISO 8549 (Parts 1–3), ISO 13405 (Parts 1–3), and ISO 10328 are particularly important. These standards provide methods and terminology for categorizing and describing products and components. National classification systems for prosthetic and orthotic products should adhere to these standards. The procurement of materials and logistics is a critical task for prosthetics and orthotics service providers. Effective management ensures cost-efficiency and uninterrupted services. In larger organizations, this may be handled by a dedicated procurement office, while smaller units may delegate this responsibility to regular staff. Components and materials may be imported or sourced locally. However, importing materials can be challenging, especially in lowand middle-income countries, due to lengthy and costly customs clearance processes. National stakeholders should collaborate with relevant authorities to exempt prosthetic and orthotic materials from import taxes and simplify importation procedures. National distribution systems for components and materials can streamline procurement processes and reduce costs. In some countries, a central procurement office and storage facility may facilitate this process. When integrated into the health system, the central store should be part of the health ministry’s medical supplies department. Bulk orders placed by a central store can reduce costs and simplify importation for individual service units. Proper stock management is essential to avoid service interruptions due to material shortages or overstocking. Effective planning ensures that all materials are in good condition and available when needed. Computer software can assist in managing stock, recording values, preparing purchase orders, and calculating service costs. In larger service units, a dedicated storekeeper should oversee stock management, and storage areas should be separate from other workshop spaces. Some service providers receive in-kind donations of components and materials from organizations or enterprises. While these donations can increase productivity, the donated items must meet the provider’s standards and be appropriate for their needs. Providers should have input into the types and quantities of donated materials to ensure they align with their requirements. Reusing prosthetic and orthotic components can reduce costs and assist more individuals. However, this practice should be regulated by the state to ensure user safety. Used products must be refurbished by licensed operators under controlled conditions, decontaminated, and approved before reuse. The process should be documented, and users must be informed when reused components are included in their devices. Customized parts, such as prosthetic sockets, should never be reused. Donations of used prostheses and orthoses from high-income countries to lowand middle-income countries are well-intentioned but not always helpful. Custom-made devices are unlikely to fit new users, and disassembled components may not be compatible with local technology. If technical personnel are not trained in the new technologies, donated components may remain unused and eventually require disposal, incurring additional costs. In-kind donations of second-hand devices should be coordinated professionally, ensuring the receiving provider can use the technology, the quality of reused components is controlled, and complete sets of items are supplied. Donations should not undermine the national market or the efforts of other service providers. Prosthetics and orthotics services generate waste, some of which may be harmful to the environment. Limiting waste during production benefits both the service provider and society. Waste materials should be disposed of according to national regulations, with hazardous products monitored closely. Users should return their devices to the service provider when no longer in use. Devices should be disassembled, reusable components salvaged, and the remainder disposed of appropriately. Prosthetics and orthotics service delivery should be regulated by the state to ensure access to high-quality products and minimize the availability of substandard, unsafe, or ineffective products. Regulations should cover product and component supply, material importation, and component reuse. ISO standards should be applied where appropriate. Structural and clinical testing of prosthetic and orthotic components and materials is essential to ensure durability and prevent device failure that could harm users. Structural testing is conducted in laboratory settings according to ISO specifications, such as ISO 10328, which outlines procedures for testing the strength of lower-limb prostheses. Standardized testing procedures enable comparisons of different components, such as prosthetic feet, in terms of quality and cost-effectiveness. Manufacturers should test new technologies before market release to demonstrate compliance with national and international standards. Clinical field tests complement structural testing by evaluating the strength, durability, functionality, safety, and effectiveness of components and products under normal use conditions. Environmental factors, such as rough terrain and hot, humid weather in low-income settings, may challenge components. Systematic user trials in the field can assess the impact of such conditions and compare alternative technologies. Clinical testing should adhere to ethical regulations, with voluntary participation and informed consent, and follow scientific standards to ensure reliable results. Research is critical for advancing prosthetics and orthotics services. However, most research benefits high-income countries, with limited attention to the needs of lowand middle-income countries. There is a lack of documented evidence on the appropriateness, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness of prosthetic and orthotic technologies and treatments. WHO has identified five priority research areas for assistive technology: effects, costs, and economic impact; policies, systems, and service delivery models; high-quality, affordable technology; human resources; and standards and methods for assessing needs and unmet needs. International organizations and academic institutions should stimulate research in these areas and facilitate the sharing of results to benefit services worldwide. At the national level, research should be conducted at centers of excellence, linked to academic training programs, and coordinated with national and international stakeholders. Systems should support research training for relevant personnel, and service providers should routinely gather and share data with researchers. The development of affordable prosthetic and orthotic products is essential to meet the needs of diverse populations. Components, materials, and consumables are produced by suppliers worldwide at various operational scales. However, most research and development in this field is conducted by enterprises in high-income countries.
